extracted.intended_audience: students and general readers of political philosophy, lawmakers, and citizens concerned with limits of social and legal authority
extracted.subtask_description: Normative criteria for when society or government may legitimately interfere with an individual's conduct. Distinguishes self-regarding from other-regarding actions and discusses the proper roles of law, public opinion, education, and punishment, with examples (prohibition, Sabbatarian laws, dietary/religious practices).

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-regarding conduct should remain free
rubrics_metrics.description: There should be perfect freedom, legal and social, to do actions which affect no persons but the agent himself (all concerned being of full age and ordinary understanding).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When conduct affects only the individual, society has no jurisdiction; persuasion and education are the appropriate instruments, not legal compulsion. Examples/anti-patterns: forbidding purely private habits (e.g., drinking by consenting adults) is unjustified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Society's jurisdiction when conduct prejudicially affects others
rubrics_metrics.description: As soon as any part of a person's conduct affects prejudicially the interests of others, society has jurisdiction and may consider interference for the general welfare.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interference (moral censure or legal sanction) is appropriate where conduct encroaches on others' rights, causes loss or damage, or involves breach of duty to specific persons or the public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punishment by opinion vs punishment by law
rubrics_metrics.description: Offences that affect only the individual's own interests may be justly punished by public opinion but not by law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Social penalties (ostracism, loss of consideration, withholding favors) are legitimate responses to self-regarding faults, but legal force should be reserved for harms to others. Scoring note: differentiate social condemnation from state-enforced punishment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interference requires definite damage or definite risk
rubrics_metrics.description: Whenever there is a definite damage, or a definite risk of damage, either to an individual or to the public, the case is taken out of the province of liberty and placed in that of morality or law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vague or merely speculative harms do not justify coercion; look for concrete, assignable injury or risk before justifying legal intervention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duties to oneself are not socially enforceable unless they affect others
rubrics_metrics.description: What are called duties to ourselves (besides prudence or self-respect) are not socially obligatory, because their aims (self-development, self-respect) are not for the good of mankind and thus are not grounds for social accountability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid claiming that private self-improvement or self-regarding prudence justifies law. Exception: if failing in self-care breaches a definite obligation to others (e.g., family support), then social reproach or punishment may be warranted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Education and persuasion preferred to compulsion
rubrics_metrics.description: Disinterested benevolence should use instruments of conviction and persuasion rather than compulsion to promote the good of others; after education, self-regarding virtues should be inculcated by persuasion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resort to compulsion only when persuasion and education cannot protect others' interests; coercion often discredits better means and breeds rebellion among independent characters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Individuality and spontaneity have a proper field
rubrics_metrics.description: In each person's own concerns, his individual spontaneity is entitled to free exercise; general rules are necessary mainly for social conduct, not for private life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow room for personal experiments in living and nonconformity; excessively rigid social or legal regulation of personal choices stifles individuality and may produce perverse reactions (e.g., deliberate opposition to usurped authority).

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural social consequences permissible, but not vindictive interference
rubrics_metrics.description: People may suffer penalties at the hands of others (loss of society, disfavour) for self-regarding faults, but these penalties should be the natural consequences of the faults, not intentionally inflicted punishments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is legitimate to avoid someone's company or prefer others for optional good offices; but making life uncomfortable purposely for the sake of punishment exceeds proper social response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acts injurious to others merit moral reprobation and possible legal punishment
rubrics_metrics.description: Encroachment on others' rights, infliction of loss or damage, falsehood, unfair advantage, or selfish abstinence from defending others are fit objects of moral reprobation and, in grave cases, of punishment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess both the act and the dispositions that lead to it (malice, cruelty, envy, dissimulation); these are proper matters for social condemnation and, where serious, legal sanction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protection of those incapable of self-government (children, minors)
rubrics_metrics.description: Society has absolute power over children and persons under age and is justified in protecting those manifestly unfit for self-government during their formative period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use education and the authority of received opinion to cultivate rational conduct in the rising generation; this does not justify coercing competent adults who had the opportunity for upbringing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bad example alone rarely justifies coercion
rubrics_metrics.description: The argument that private misconduct should be controlled because it serves as a bad example to others is generally insufficient to justify coercion, except where the example involves doing wrong to others with impunity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the example produces real pernicious effects; in many cases the display of misconduct also reveals its degrading consequences, making example more salutary than harmful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public opinion and majorities are unreliable grounds for coercion in self-regarding matters
rubrics_metrics.description: On questions of self-regarding conduct, public opinion is at least as likely to be wrong as right and often simply reflects the public's personal tastes rather than a legitimate concern for others' interests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be wary of translating majority distaste or taste-based preferences into legal prohibition; the public's personal feelings are not parity with rights against harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public taste is not a legitimate basis for legislation
rubrics_metrics.description: A person's taste (what offends or disgusts others) is as much his own peculiar concern as his opinion or purse, and cannot justify law that enforces conformity to that taste.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples cited: dietary customs (eating pork), religious practices, marriage choices; laws based solely on majority disgust or preference are unjustifiable and amount to persecution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection of the 'social rights' doctrine that legitimizes coercion to enforce moral perfection
rubrics_metrics.description: The doctrine that every individual has a vested social right that others must act exactly as he thinks fit is monstrous and would justify any violation of liberty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reject policies that claim a universal right to demand others' moral, intellectual, or physical perfection as grounds for legislative coercion; it permits unlimited interference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sabbatarian and religiously motivated restrictions require narrow justification
rubrics_metrics.description: Restrictions on Sunday amusements and similar Sabbatarian legislation can only be defended when they protect the direct interests of others (e.g., preventing imposition on laborers), not because the amusements are religiously wrong.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If restriction is justified, prefer non-religious mechanisms (customary holidays, compensation) rather than laws grounded in religious morality. Anti-pattern: invoking religious duty to justify general prohibitions on amusements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition of conduct as an improper method to preserve future generations
rubrics_metrics.description: Arguments that law should forbid vices (e.g., gambling, drunkenness) to prevent future generations from repeating past errors fail if the only ground is that experience shows such conduct unwise; coercion is not justified merely to prevent repetition of known follies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer education, social opinion, and upbringing to legal prohibition; coercion risks wrong application and suppression of individuality without necessarily preventing the vice effectively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider individual knowledge and particular circumstances before applying general presumptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Interference of society to overrule an individual's judgment in his private concerns must be grounded on general presumptions, which are likely to be wrong or misapplied because outsiders lack the individual's particular knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy or law should account for the risk of misapplication of general rules to individual cases; deference to personal judgment is warranted where outside actors are not better acquainted with the facts.
